subject: ELA
title: Goodall: evidence changes an explanation
teach: Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.

model.prompt: An original parallel case: An observer sees a crow bend wire and use it to lift a food basket. What claim can she support?
model.reasoning: Separate observed behavior: the crow changed wire and used it. Make a limited claim: this crow modified an object for a task. Reject the overclaim: one observation does not prove every crow does this. Ask what would strengthen the claim: repeated observations, more individuals and conditions.
model.answer: The observation supports that this crow modified an object to obtain food. It does not establish that every crow does so; repeated varied observations would test the broader claim.

guided.prompt: Original case: A student sees one ant move a seed. Which is a directly observed action?
options: The ant moved a seed.
All ants prefer that seed.
The ant planned a garden.
No other food was nearby.
guided.rationale: Only the stated action is directly observed; the other claims add interpretation or missing evidence.

practice.prompt: Source context: David strips leaves from a twig and uses it to collect termites. Which claim is directly supported?
options: Humans learned tool-making from David.
All animals make tools.
Every chimp uses the same tool.
David changed an object to make it useful.
practice.rationale: The modification and use support the limited claim about David; the other claims exceed the described observation.

repair.teach: The modification and use support the limited claim about David; the other claims exceed the described observation. Goodall’s memoir explains how understanding developed through patient observation, setbacks, relationships and records. Read the assigned paragraphs, then ask: what did she observe, what did she infer, and what changed?
repair.prompt: Original case: One camera records a fox at dusk. Which is the best-supported claim?
options: Every camera always works.
No fox visits in daylight.
All foxes are active only at dusk.
A fox was recorded at dusk at that site.
repair.rationale: The observation supports a limited claim about that record.

practice.prompt: Source context: Goodall writes field observations in a notebook and rewrites them legibly each evening. Why is this relevant to reliable research?
options: It preserves details before memory fades.
It replaces the need to observe again.
It makes the research a fictional story.
It prevents every possible mistake.
practice.rationale: Organized prompt recording preserves evidence; it does not guarantee perfect accuracy.

repair.teach: Organized prompt recording preserves evidence; it does not guarantee perfect accuracy. Goodall’s memoir explains how understanding developed through patient observation, setbacks, relationships and records. Read the assigned paragraphs, then ask: what did she observe, what did she infer, and what changed?
repair.prompt: A class compares two plant treatments. Which action improves the evidence record?
options: Remove unexpected results.
Record conditions, measurements and dates consistently.
Write only the result that looks best.
Rely on memory a month later.
repair.rationale: Consistent records preserve relevant conditions and results.

practice.prompt: Which detail is most relevant to a claim that the research grew into organized teamwork?
options: Bananas were available.
The forest was thick.
The original tent was old.
Assistants helped record observations and the camp became a research center.
practice.rationale: Assistants and the center directly show expansion and shared work.

repair.teach: Assistants and the center directly show expansion and shared work. Goodall’s memoir explains how understanding developed through patient observation, setbacks, relationships and records. Read the assigned paragraphs, then ask: what did she observe, what did she infer, and what changed?
repair.prompt: A claim concerns teamwork. Which original detail is most relevant?
options: The tent has two poles.
The sky was cloudy.
The notebook cover is green.
Several observers share and compare records of the same events.
repair.rationale: The detail provides direct evidence of coordinated work.

practice.prompt: A student says, “One surprising event proves all earlier ideas are wrong.” Which response is strongest?
options: Ignore observations that disagree with earlier ideas.
Explain exactly which belief the observation challenges and what further evidence is needed.
Use a stronger adjective instead of evidence.
Agree because surprising events are always conclusive.
practice.rationale: Evidence can revise a particular explanation; it does not automatically overturn unrelated claims.

repair.teach: Evidence can revise a particular explanation; it does not automatically overturn unrelated claims. Goodall’s memoir explains how understanding developed through patient observation, setbacks, relationships and records. Read the assigned paragraphs, then ask: what did she observe, what did she infer, and what changed?
repair.prompt: An account shows one artist improving through practice. What further evidence is needed for a claim about all artists?
options: The same example repeated.
No evidence is needed.
Observations across more artists, tasks and conditions.
A brighter cover.
repair.rationale: One case cannot establish a universal pattern.

independentCheck.prompt: A researcher records three chimp visits at one tree. Which conclusion is appropriately limited?
options: No other tree provides food.
The observations prove the animals can speak.
All chimps always use this tree.
These visits show use of this tree during the observed period.
independentCheck.rationale: State what the actual observations establish; broader patterns need broader evidence.

repair.prompt: One tagged dolphin visits a bay twice in a week. Which conclusion stays within the observation?
options: All dolphins always live in this bay.
The observations prove dolphins speak human language.
No dolphin uses any other location.
This dolphin visited this bay during the observed week.
repair.rationale: State what the observations establish; a species-wide pattern requires broader evidence.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: State what the actual observations establish; broader patterns need broader evidence. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

independentCheck.prompt: A student claims accurate records matter. Which Goodall detail is relevant?
options: She rewrote notes legibly while the day’s observations were fresh.
The narrator likes a view.
The story has61 paragraphs.
The tent was old.
independentCheck.rationale: The detail directly concerns preserving observations.

repair.prompt: An original research report argues that accurate records matter. Which detail is relevant?
options: The field station had a pleasant view.
Each measurement was dated and checked against the original reading.
The notebook had a colorful cover.
The researcher’s coat was blue.
repair.rationale: The relevant detail concerns preserving and checking observations, not merely sharing the setting.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: The detail directly concerns preserving observations. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

independentCheck.prompt: What is the difference between a plausible inference and a directly observed action?
options: An inference interprets evidence; an observed action reports what happened.
An action is always an opinion.
An inference never uses evidence.
They are always identical.
independentCheck.rationale: An interpretation may be reasonable without being the directly recorded event.

repair.prompt: Original observation: a bird left its branch when a hawk approached. Which statement is an inference rather than the directly observed movement?
options: The bird left the branch.
A hawk approached the tree.
The observer recorded the movement.
The bird may have moved to avoid a threat.
repair.rationale: Avoiding a threat interprets a possible reason; the movement and approach are directly reported events.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: An interpretation may be reasonable without being the directly recorded event. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

independentCheck.prompt: A video shows one successful experiment. What question best tests a broad claim based on it?
options: Which filter is prettiest?
Can the title be longer?
Who has the most followers?
What happened in repeated trials under different conditions?
independentCheck.rationale: Repeated varied tests can reveal reliability and boundaries.

repair.prompt: A video shows one battery lasting longer in one device. What would best test a broad claim that it is always superior?
options: Repeated comparisons across relevant devices and conditions.
A more dramatic title on the video.
A claim repeated by more viewers without testing.
The color of the camera used.
repair.rationale: A broad reliability claim needs evidence across relevant trials and boundaries.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: Repeated varied tests can reveal reliability and boundaries. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

delayed.prompt: Original observation: one plant grows more in a sunny window than in shade. Which conclusion is most careful?
options: One trial proves the entire mechanism.
The sunny plant grew more in this comparison; more controlled trials are needed.
Every plant needs identical light.
Shade kills all plants.
delayed.rationale: Limit the claim to the comparison and identify evidence needed.

repair.prompt: In one dry-surface trial, one shoe gripped better than another. Which conclusion is careful?
options: The shoe gripped better under the tested dry conditions; other conditions remain untested.
The result proves performance on wet ice.
That shoe prevents every possible fall.
One trial explains every shoe design.
repair.rationale: Limit the claim to the comparison and state what additional conditions need investigation.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: Limit the claim to the comparison and identify evidence needed. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

delayed.prompt: Which evidence best supports a claim that a writer’s process became more organized?
options: The writer’s height.
A favorite snack.
Dated notes arranged and checked after each session.
A colorful cover.
delayed.rationale: The evidence directly concerns organization of the work.

repair.prompt: Which detail best supports a claim that an investigation became more organized?
options: The team bought a new snack.
The box holding supplies was larger.
The team introduced dated logs and checked entries after each session.
The team selected a favorite color.
repair.rationale: The logging and checking concern organization directly.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: The evidence directly concerns organization of the work. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

delayed.prompt: An inference goes beyond direct observation by doing what?
options: Removing all facts.
Copying every word.
Becoming certain without support.
Interpreting what evidence may mean.

repair.prompt: Two seedlings grew at different rates. A student says the difference may reflect unequal light. What is she doing?
options: Reporting the light measurements, although none were taken.
Offering an interpretation that needs evidence about light conditions.
Proving all growth differences have one cause.
Removing every observed fact from the account.
repair.rationale: An inference can be plausible without being the directly measured event or a certain causal proof.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: Inference explains or interprets evidence. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

delayed.prompt: A student says an explanation is certain although key measurements are missing. What should she do?
options: Guess the missing values.
Name the uncertainty and gather the needed measurements.
Hide the gap.
State the conclusion more loudly.
delayed.rationale: Acknowledging and investigating an evidence gap improves reasoning.

repair.prompt: A report claims a certain result although an important quantity was never measured. What is the strongest next step?
options: Name the uncertainty and collect the missing relevant measurements.
Hide the missing measurement in a longer title.
Guess the value and present it as recorded.
Repeat the claim more confidently.
repair.rationale: Evidence gaps should limit confidence and guide further investigation rather than be concealed.
repair.teach: Return to the saved response: Acknowledging and investigating an evidence gap improves reasoning. Explain which condition or evidence supports the answer, then apply it to the different case below.

proof.prompt: Return to assigned paragraphs 38–39 and46. Write a claim about how careful observation supports scientific learning. Accurately paraphrase one detail from each section, explain each link, and identify one conclusion those details cannot establish. Then apply the same reasoning to a claim about a sewing technique.
criteria: Accurate claim limited to the evidence
Two accurate paragraph-linked details
Explains why each detail supports claim
Names a real evidence limit
Applies evidence/limit reasoning to unfamiliar sewing example

bridge.prompt: A claim says a design works. Does naming the material prove the claim? Explain the missing step.
bridge.explanation: A relevant detail needs a reason linking it to the claim. A material’s name alone does not establish performance; describe observed results and their limits.

links.laterApplication: Use this idea again without notes after 1, 3, 7, 14 and 30 days. Explain a new example and a limit; familiar wording alone does not prove understanding.

studyMap:
Original study map of the assigned Goodall memoir (paragraphs 1–61)

Paragraphs1–17 establish the beginning and obstacles. Goodall arrives at Gombe with her mother and a small support team. Early observation is frustrating because the chimps avoid people. She changes how she watches and gradually learns their movements, food and grouping. The repeated unsuccessful days and the contrast with faster-adjusting baboons make the difficulty clear.

Paragraphs18–30 develop her knowledge of the environment and the support behind the work. She encounters risks, observes daily behavior and describes help from her mother, local people and others. Research depends on relationships as well as persistence.

Paragraphs31–39 mark an important change. David Greybeard visits camp and becomes more comfortable near her. Other chimps gradually allow closer observation. She sees David use grass and modify a twig to collect termites. The observation challenges a prior assumption about human tool-making.

Paragraphs40–46 include changing weather, danger and recordkeeping. Goodall rewrites observations legibly while the day’s details are fresh.

Paragraphs47–59 describe individual temperaments, family life, communication and social behavior. National Geographic sends Hugo van Lawick to film the work. Goodall studies at Cambridge, earns her Ph.D. and returns to Gombe.

Paragraphs60–61 show increasing records, helpers and a research center. The ending connects the small beginning to sustained organized research. This study aid supports source-return analysis; read the complete assigned selection for its wording and details.

teachingSections.title: Explain what she learned about chimps
teach: Goodall learned that chimps use tools and can change materials to make tools. David stripped leaves from a twig before using it to get termites.
She learned that chimps are individuals. They have different personalities, and their family relationships affect how they act.
She also saw young chimps learning from others. Chimps use calls and gestures to share information. Some gestures look like human gestures, but their calls are not the same as human language.
When you explain a discovery, tell what she saw and what it helped her understand. Do not make a bigger claim than the detail supports.
teachingSections.where: Readings → PDF page6, paragraphs38–39 (tools); page8, paragraphs48–54 (individuals and family); page9, paragraphs55–56 (learning, calls and gestures).

example.prompt: What did Goodall learn about chimp communication?
example.thinking: I reread paragraph56. Then I explain what the calls and gestures show without claiming that chimps speak just like humans.
example.answer: Goodall learned that chimps share information through calls and gestures. In paragraph56, she describes signals that help chimps know what is happening. Some gestures look like ours, but their calls do not form a language in the same way human words do.
example.why: It explains a discovery, points to a paragraph, and keeps the claim accurate.

teachingSections.tryPrompt: What is the difference between using a tool and making a tool?
teachingSections.tryAnswer: Using a tool means using an object to do a job. Making a tool means changing material so it can do the job, as David did when he removed leaves from a twig.
